what_it_did.what_the_split_means: A mechanical commit republishes an unchanged net -- the report, the dashboard, the state files. Counting those as work would make a quiet day look busy, so they are separated rather than filtered: they happened, they are just not progress.

what_it_decided.thesis_read: Three hours, 21 commits, nine substantive, and the thesis got its first honest answer on the right population: it is NEGATIVE, and that is the stretch working rather than failing. The director asked at 09:23Z to "fix the renewal schedule and rerun the A/B" and both landed. The schedule bug was real and large -- `roll_lifecycle_event` returned `None` for every renewal whose month fell past the settled window, so whether a customer ever got a churn decision depended on whether their anniversary fell on the 31st or the 1st, and six of the nine residential seed accounts were priced at eighteen renewals and produced not one lifecycle event. Repaired, `scored_share_of_priced` goes 57.1% to 100.0%, the arm's advantage survives and more than halves to +£7,066 settled, and the belief-quality result does not survive at all: `discrimination_auc` falls from 0.6944 to 0.4653 -- below a coin flip -- and it is not uniform noise, it is INVERTED in the middle of the arm's own range (believed p_retain 0.346 realised 0.818 on n=11; believed 0.616 realised 0.000 on n=4). Read beside the same artefact's other fields -- a median margin of £44.50/MWh against the flat rule's £2.00, 24% of priced renewals decided by a bound rather than by the model, and 15 of 211 accounts carrying 99.3% of the movement -- the honest sentence is that this company raised prices 22x on a handful of accounts whose staying-or-leaving it could not predict. That is a claim about the book's price elasticity, not about the company's belief, and the advantage is therefore NOT yet attributable to inference. It is exactly the result the director said he wanted: a negative result on the right population is worth more than a £3M headline on the wrong one. Two of the four focus items are finished and gone from this list -- the full-window instruments were sized (559.8s per pass measured, 2.85 GB peak, against a 632s upper bound) and the full-window A/B ran and now names its book; and the director's 33 reds are reconciled to the node id, all closed, with the reason his 33 and the machine's 28 were never the same population. The machine also caught two of its own errors before either was published -- a 9.4x level-vs-selection headline that was two confounds, and a 15.8% "cap breach" that was fixed-term contracts running lawfully through a cap change. What has not moved: EP1 was named for the sixth time and not worked, and its instruction went stale within the hour, because `353fe96b8` changed the very estimator its ledger grades while that ledger still reads `measured_at: 2026-08-26T11:46:22Z`. EP13 was given the company half for the fourth time and delivered SIM-side work for the fourth time, and its own cheap close was unbuildable as written. And one claim published this morning at 04:45 -- "the ladder: the win is NOT price" -- was measured on the broken schedule, over a common population of six decisions, and nothing in the document says so. Correcting that is the first thing this direction owes a reader.

focus.what: Build a HARNESS instrument that grades the company's renewal churn belief against the world's realised outcome over EVERY renewal in a full-window control run, not the 25 the value arm happened to price. For each renewal the world rolled, compute the company's own believed probability the way the desk does -- `saas/churn_model.build_churn_risk(settlement_records, customers, through_period=<the month being priced>)`, using only records observable before that month -- and pair it with the world's logged lifecycle event. Publish, per believed-probability bucket: n, mean believed, realised rate, and the count of accounts behind it. Then answer the one question in a sentence with the evidence attached: is the inversion at believed p_retain 0.35-0.62 real at population scale, or is it n=4 and n=11? If it is real, name the MECHANISM -- `build_churn_risk` is `BASE_ANNUAL_CHURN_PROBABILITY + k x CHURN_UPLIFT_PER_BILL_SHOCK`, so the candidate is that bill shock predicts the opposite of what the model assumes on this book, and that is testable directly from the same pairs. Re-state the ladder's level error (believed 33% against a realised 5.5%) on this population and say whether it survives. Do NOT change `BASE_CHURN_RATE`, `CHURN_UPLIFT_PER_BILL_SHOCK` or any cap in this item -- R12, the AUC is a diagnostic and never a thing to move. File the table as a finding under `docs/staging/` and bind the paths with `delivery_lane.record_landing` as each piece lands.
focus.why: This is the engine of the thesis and it is currently measured at below a coin flip on 25 decisions. Four separately published numbers all rest on this one belief -- the A/B's 0.4653 AUC, the ladder's 33%-vs-5.5% level error, EP1's collapsed hazard, and the arm's -0.077 calibration error -- and every one of them was measured on a population small enough or broken enough to be an artefact. One instrument diagnoses all four at once, which is why it goes first under COMPOUNDING_WORK_FIRST. It is also the cheapest decisive thing available: it grades an existing company function against an outcome the world already logs, changes no company code, and cannot fail to produce a finding. Finished when the bucketed table exists as a named artefact over a population an order of magnitude larger than 25, and the document says whether the inversion is real and, if it is, what causes it. "The belief has no ranking power on this book and here is why" is a complete and valuable answer; so is "the inversion was n=4". Do not repair the estimator in the same act -- diagnose, then stop, and let the repair be drawn on the evidence.

focus.what: Build the third arm properly, inside `renewal_margin_uplift`, exactly as `docs/staging/done/WORKER_FINDING_THE_LEVEL_VS_SELECTION_TEST_CANNOT_BE_BUILT_FROM_THE_FLAT_CONSTANT_2026-08-27.md` specifies: apply a FLAT uplift of the value arm's own realised median (`decision_shape.median_margin_gbp_per_mwh` = 44.50) at exactly the renewals the value arm prices, under the same lawful ceiling the value arm is held to. Do not override `TARGET_MARGIN_GBP_PER_MWH` -- that route was built, run and withdrawn in this stretch and it raises the base tariff of the whole book while the value arm's uplift touches 25 renewals, so it changes the population as well as the level, and it lets one arm price above the Ofgem cap while the other is clamped. Run it against the same book and seeds as `value_cycle_ab_resi_renewal_fixed.json` and report the three nets side by side. Then say which branch is true, in the artefact's own words: if flat-at-£44.50 reproduces the £7,066 the arm is a price rise wearing a model; if it does not, the per-customer variation is worth something even at AUC 0.4653 and the next question is what it is picking up. While you are in `decide_margin`, the FLAT branch's unguarded ceiling -- it returns before the `lawful` filter, so it CAN offer above the cap where the value arm cannot -- is a real latent defect and this arm makes it bite; fix it or state why it cannot. R15: mutation-test the new arm both ways, and the mutation that matters is the one that makes it a no-op.

entries.what: A claim published this morning is standing on a defect the same document proves fatal five hours later, and nothing says so. The section "the ladder: the win is NOT price" was measured at 04:45Z on `value_cycle_price_ladder_2019.json`; the renewal-schedule repair landed at `353fe96b8` around 09:49Z. Observed: that artefact's own `unmatched_diagnosis` records 18 decisions the world never rolled and 6 accounts it never rolled at all, and its two slopes are computed over a common population of six decisions. Inferred, and the inference is short: this is the identical mechanism that the renewal-repair section shows invalidated the sibling `discrimination_auc` of 0.6944, so the ladder's headline is at best unproven. Nobody has been wrong on purpose here -- the repair simply landed after the reading -- but a reader of that document today is told the price question is answered, and it is not.

EP1 was named for the sixth time and not worked, and this time the instruction was partly at fault: it was written against `coupled_gap_ledger.json`'s EP1 row, and `353fe96b8` changed `saas/churn_model.build_churn_risk` -- the estimator that row grades -- within the hour, while the row still reads `measured_at: 2026-08-26T11:46:22Z` at `run_git_commit: 8afa34ceb`. A direction that names a measurement should say what invalidates it; mine did not, so a worker drawing it would have spent the tick diagnosing a number that no longer describes the code. The re-measure is now the first act of the item rather than the assumed background.

The level-vs-selection tool was built, run, and returned a 9.4x headline that was an artefact twice over, and it was withdrawn in the same turn before anything was published. Confound one: `decide_margin`'s FLAT branch returns before the `lawful` filter, so the counterfactual let one arm offer £39.50 above the cap while clamping the other. Confound two, and fatal to the approach: `renewal_margin_uplift` returns `MarginArmUplift(0.0)` for FLAT_RULES, so overriding `TARGET_MARGIN_GBP_PER_MWH` raised the base tariff of every contract rather than the 25 renewals the value arm priced. Recorded as an error rather than a save because several hours went into a route whose second confound was readable in the adapter's first three lines -- but the catch itself was the right move and took two minutes, made by asking what the number would have to mean for it to be true.

A 15.8% breach rate against the Ofgem cap was measured -- 28,093 of 178,229 domestic electricity settlement records above `get_cap_unit_rate_for_date` -- and was two minutes from being reported as a compliance finding. It is not one: the default-tariff cap binds the OFFER and does not reach backwards into a live fixed term, and `PROS-2019-0050` carries exactly one rate, £188.59, across its whole breach window, which is a locked term and not a default tariff drifting. The comparison was settled rates against a rule that governs offers. Caught, and the narrower real question -- does the flat arm ever OFFER above the cap at a renewal -- is now item two's second clause. The pattern is worth keeping: three measurement designs in one investigation each ran perfectly and answered a question nobody had asked.

EP13 was given the company half for the fourth stretch and delivered the world half for the fourth time, and the instruction was unbuildable in its cheap-close branch: it directed the worker to write the "no company consumer exists" statement into the maturity-map entry, which sits at 11,940 B against a 12,288 B per-atom cap, so that write would have refused the commit tree-wide. Four failed namings with a defect in the naming is a pattern in the instruction, not in the tick. The fifth version has one act, ten minutes, and a landing place that can accept it.

All three focus items went unworked, and the previous orientation's framing would have called that a fifth consecutive stall. It was not one and saying so matters more than the tally: the director's console at 05:39Z reported 33 newly failing tests, and the machine correctly dropped the direction to answer him -- 28 reds closed, the responder-side secret redaction he asked for built and wired at nine call sites, `tools/wait_for.py` and R18 landed against his third-time-this-week waiter complaint. A direction displaced by the director is the direction working. The error I am recording is in the DIRECTION, not the machine: three items totalling several hours of compute were written into a three-hour stretch that also had to absorb whatever he sent, and nothing in the file said which item to drop first if it did. This one has four items and each one names a cheap outcome that counts as finished.

EP1's diagnosis has been wrong five times, and my predecessor's correction of the first four was wrong too. Four instructions said "widen the hazard's inputs". The fifth said "the hazard is borrowed from `saas/churn_model.build_churn_risk`, change whose it is". I verified that chain and it holds -- `simulation/customer_events.py:152` does import it and it does feed the world's realised churn -- but it is not the explanation, because the shared estimator is not thin. Over 622 renewal decisions it publishes 13 distinct hazards spanning 0.05 to 0.41 (mean 0.183, only 263 at the base), and the same run's graded 33 all recover exactly 0.05 across nine belief years. Observed: both figures from `coupled_gap_ledger.json`'s own `hazard_calibration` and `lifetime_level` blocks, and the 13 values are exactly `BASE_ANNUAL_CHURN_PROBABILITY + k x CHURN_UPLIFT_PER_BILL_SHOCK` for k = 0..12. Inferred: that `LATEST_RENEWAL_CONDITIONED` at `clv_three_horizon.py:580` is the collapse point, which is a hypothesis item one is written to test rather than assume. Five namings proposed a cure without a diagnosis; this one buys the diagnosis and stops.

`run_value_cycle_ab` has not run for five stretches. The escape hatch my predecessor wrote into the last instruction -- errors become the deliverable, land after each, bind the paths -- did not help, because the failure was never the instruction's wording. Two Lane 0 ticks claimed it and dropped it with no paths bound, and nobody has measured whether a full-window run FITS in the tick that keeps claiming it. what_next.why_this_is_here: Direction multiplies the draw's existing weights and can never zero one, so it can only ever be ignored -- never obeyed by force. Whether it was actually followed is therefore a measurement, not an assumption.
